kaigo-atomic-pressure-context.heading: Two blood-pressure values and measurement circumstances
paragraphs: Blood pressure is the pressure blood exerts on arterial walls. Systolic pressure is the value when the heart contracts and pumps blood; diastolic pressure is the value as it relaxes between beats. ‘Maximum’ and ‘minimum’ distinguish two values within a heartbeat.

Do not reinterpret systolic pressure as the disease hypertension or diastolic pressure as hypotension. Record both as a pair, separately from disease assessment. This lesson does not establish new diagnostic thresholds.

Blood pressure varies during the day. Posture, activity, emotional state and illness can affect it, so one measurement does not remain unchanged all day. Record known conditions such as time, posture and activity beforehand.

Check circumstances such as excitement, tension, poor sleep, sudden exercise or temperature changes when pressure varies. Straining during bowel movements or holding urine or stool can also be relevant. Do not ask the person to delay toileting for staff schedules.

If two blood-pressure readings differ and the second was taken immediately after activity, report both values and the circumstances of each measurement separately. Do not dismiss an unusual reading because it followed activity or conclude from that reading alone that hypertension has developed or resolved. Follow the individual care plan and facility procedures for the contact or rechecking required by the person’s condition.

kaigo-atomic-pressure-organs.heading: Vessels and organs affected by hypertension
paragraphs: Persistently high blood pressure can strain blood vessels and organs. Hypertension may occur without symptoms such as headache, so no pain does not establish normal pressure. Actual measurements and healthcare assessment are needed. Contributing factors can include lifestyle and heredity, or another illness such as kidney disease. High blood pressure can burden the heart, but this does not mean every heart disease causes hypertension. Do not decide causes from disease names alone; check healthcare professionals’ assessment.

In the brain, distinguish an ischemic stroke caused by a blocked vessel from diseases involving bleeding from a ruptured vessel. Bleeding includes intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhage. Learning these names differs from a care worker diagnosing the person’s symptoms.
In the heart, coronary blood-flow problems can lead to angina or myocardial infarction. Arteriosclerosis involves changes in vessel walls; it is not the name of one blood-pressure value.

Retinal vessels may also be affected. Healthcare professionals assess the brain, eyes, kidneys and overall vascular condition as well as the heart. Absence of one symptom does not establish that other organs are unaffected.

Follow the person’s treatment and support plan for salt intake, activity and medication. Even if they feel well, care workers do not independently stop or change medication doses. The role is to communicate measurements, changes from usual and the person’s words specifically.

kaigo-atomic-body-regions.heading: Accurately communicate body locations
paragraphs: Major body regions are the head, neck, trunk, upper limbs and lower limbs. The trunk includes the chest and abdomen. ‘My arm hurts’ covers a broad area, so check the indicated location and the person’s own words and specify the side. Use the person’s body, rather than the worker’s viewpoint, to define left and right.

The inner eye corner is the end near the nose; the outer corner is on the opposite side. The forehead is the upper facial area and the chin the lower area. Also distinguish the external neck from the throat, checking where the person means.

The arm, wrist, fingers and fingertips cover different areas. The palm and back of the hand are different surfaces too. When reporting pain or an area cleaned, use the correct name for the confirmed area rather than only ‘hand.’
Distinguish ankle, toes and heel. The sole and underside of the foot refer to the lower surface, opposite the top of the foot. Check which surface is meant.

The lower back does not mean the entire back. Buttocks and the everyday word ‘bottom’ refer to the same area. ‘Affected side’ refers to a side with impairment; ‘unaffected side’ is used in contrast. Neither fixes left or right, and ‘unaffected’ does not guarantee no problems at all.

In a report, distinguish the body location, side, time and the person’s own words. If you have not yet asked about the intensity or cause of pain, do not fill the gaps with assumptions. When a sudden change or another circumstance requires contact, do not delay reporting until you have finished every question.

kaigo-atomic-nerves.heading: Nerves connecting the center and periphery
paragraphs: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. Peripheral nerves carry information between the center and body regions. The brain receives and processes bodily information, contributes to judgment and sends necessary instructions.

The usual classification counts 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. A pair is a unit of two. Writing only ‘12 nerves’ or ‘31 nerves’ changes the counting unit and loses the paired meaning.

Sensory information travels from the body to the center; motor commands travel from the center to the body. The spinal cord carries information upward and downward and participates in responses such as reflexes. This is not a solely downward command system.

In body-distribution diagrams, distinguish location labels such as head, chest and lower back from classifications such as cranial and spinal nerves. A location name is not automatically the name of one nerve pair.

This explanation teaches information direction and classification. Do not identify causes of numbness or movement difficulty from a diagram alone. Communicate location, timing and the person’s own words and arrange individual assessment.

kaigo-atomic-brain-parts.heading: Brain regions and their functions
paragraphs: The cerebrum supports information understanding and conscious activity. The cerebellum contributes to balance and movement coordination. Connect each diagram region with its function rather than treating every part simply as ‘brain.’

The midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata are parts of the brainstem. It contributes to life-maintaining functions such as heartbeat, breathing and swallowing. Confirm the pons as part of the brainstem classification, beyond memorizing its location.

The diencephalon includes the thalamus and hypothalamus. The hypothalamus helps regulate autonomic function, temperature and sleep. Do not interchange diencephalon, cerebellum and brainstem as identical terms.

Brain regions work together, so one daily action or emotion is not determined by one location alone. Model and diagram labels provide basic knowledge, not a procedure for independently diagnosing injury locations from symptoms.

kaigo-atomic-autonomic-heart.heading: Autonomic nerves, heartbeat, vessels and blood pressure
paragraphs: The autonomic nervous system adjusts internal-organ functions without a separate conscious command for every action. Sympathetic functions are prominent in activity and tension; parasympathetic functions relate to rest and recovery. Understand both as situational regulation systems.
In the heart, sympathetic activity tends to increase heart rate and parasympathetic activity to reduce it. This general tendency does not determine the person’s actual pulse at that moment.

Sympathetic nerves also contribute to the tone of many peripheral vessels and can act toward constriction. Blood pressure involves several factors, including heart and vessels. Avoid a simplistic model in which both systems act identically in opposite directions in every organ.

Sympathetic activity may be prominent during activity, worry, anger or tension. Parasympathetic involvement matters during rest and sleep, but actual regulation depends on condition and circumstances. Disturbed autonomic regulation can affect mind and body, but one concern does not establish a diagnosis.

Appearing anxious provides information about emotional state, not a measured fact of increased blood pressure. Record numbers only for actual measurements and their conditions. Do not fill unmeasured results from general physiological tendencies.

kaigo-atomic-autonomic-other.heading: Consider autonomic function by organ
paragraphs: Pupils are regulated toward dilation by sympathetic activity and constriction by parasympathetic activity. This teaches a mechanism affecting light entry, not an instruction to conduct neurological tests on the person.

In the digestive tract, sympathetic activity tends to inhibit movement, while parasympathetic activity supports digestion. Do not explain eating or bowel patterns entirely through one nerve name; also check personal condition and daily-life information.

For airways, learn sympathetic-related effects as tending to widen bronchi and parasympathetic effects as tending to narrow them. Many factors affect actual breathing, so this classification alone does not determine breathlessness causes or medication choices.

Sympathetic signals to eccrine sweat glands are important in sweating regulation. Even if a learning table contrasts more and less sweating, do not reinterpret it as a perfectly symmetric system in which parasympathetic nerves directly stop sweat glands.

Autonomic tables model regulation direction for a particular organ. Two opposing arrows cannot explain every function throughout the body. Separate observations from assumed causes and consult professionals when needed.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-pressure-contex.prompt: Two blood-pressure readings differ; the second was immediately after activity. Which report is most appropriate?
options: Give both readings and each time, posture and activity context without assuming a diagnosis.
Systolic pressure is the pressure value when the heart contracts.
The brain and spinal cord are part of the central nervous system.
The cerebellum contributes to balance and movement coordination.
rationales: Recording conditions as well as values gives healthcare professionals information for assessing change.
The definition is correct but does not answer how to report both readings and conditions.
This describes nervous-system classification and omits measurement circumstances.
This explains cerebellar function, not the report needed for differing measurements.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-pressure-organs.prompt: Does absence of headache establish that the person does not have hypertension?
options: Blood pressure has systolic and diastolic values.
The retina receives light.
No. Symptoms may be absent; follow actual measurements and healthcare assessment.
Food nutrients are mainly absorbed in the small intestine.
rationales: Describing two values does not answer whether absent symptoms rule out hypertension.
Retinal function does not answer judging pressure from symptoms alone.
Hypertension can lack noticeable symptoms, so no headache cannot replace measurement and assessment.
Digestion and absorption do not explain the relationship between headache absence and blood-pressure assessment.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-body-regions.prompt: When handing over ‘My arm hurts,’ which information makes it specific?
options: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
Check precise location, side, timing and the person’s words.
Systole is heart contraction; diastole is relaxation.
There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
rationales: Blood-flow direction does not locate the reported pain.
This clarifies location, information source and time without inventing unchecked severity or cause.
The heartbeat cycle leaves the painful arm location unclear.
Nerve-count units do not make this pain handoff more specific.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-nerves.prompt: Cranial and spinal nerves were written as 12 and 31 individual nerves. Which correction matches the source classification?
options: Group pons, midbrain and medulla within the brainstem.
Record left and right from the person’s body.
Report blood-pressure values separately from measurement circumstances.
Use pair units:12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
rationales: The brain classification is correct but does not correct the count-unit error.
Side reference differs from nerve-count units.
Blood-pressure reporting does not correct counting nerves in pairs.
The source counts two as a pair, so correct the unit as well as the numbers.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-brain-parts.prompt: Which brain classification includes the pons?
options: The central nervous system contains brain and spinal cord.
The cerebellum supports movement coordination and balance.
The brainstem, together with midbrain and medulla.
The diencephalon contains thalamus and hypothalamus.
rationales: This broad classification does not identify the pons–brainstem relationship.
This explains cerebellar function; the pons is not the cerebellum itself.
This identifies the pons as a brainstem component, distinct from cerebrum and cerebellum in the diagram.
Diencephalic structures differ from the brainstem containing the pons.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-autonomic-heart.prompt: The person reports anxiety. May you record ‘blood pressure increased’ without measuring?
options: No. Record the anxiety separately from actually measured pressure.
Sympathetic nerves contribute to activity and tension responses.
Parasympathetic nerves contribute to regulation during rest.
The heart has right and left atria and ventricles.
rationales: General physiology must not become an unmeasured personal value or change.
This tendency does not justify recording unmeasured pressure.
Rest-related neural function does not answer separating the anxiety from measurement facts.
Heart structure is separate from recording values not measured.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-autonomic-other.prompt: Why can’t autonomic activity in every organ be represented by two perfectly opposing arrows?
options: Cerebrum and cerebellum are different parts.
Left and right use the person’s body as reference.
Systolic and diastolic pressure are recorded as a pair.
Innervation and regulation vary by organ; sympathetic activity is important in sweat glands.
rationales: Brain regions do not explain differences in autonomic organ innervation.
Side reference does not explain why sympathetic and parasympathetic effects are not universally symmetric.
Paired pressure readings differ from nerve supply to organs such as sweat glands.
Do not model parasympathetic nerves as directly stopping sweat glands; identify the organ and the model’s limits.
